html:
In 1823 the Scottish trader Robert Bruce was shown tea growing wild in the hills of Assam, in northeast India, by a chief of the Singpho people, who already brewed it.

At the time Britain bought all its tea from China and paid with silver, and later with opium, which led toward the First Opium War. Finding tea in a land the East India Company was just taking over in 1826 looked like a way out.

Botanists in Calcutta at first doubted it was real tea. Bruce's brother Charles kept sending samples, and in the 1830s the plant was accepted as a local variety of Camellia sinensis, now called assamica. It has larger leaves and gives a strong, dark brew. The first Assam tea was sold in London in 1839.

The Assam Company was formed the same year to grow it. The British went on to plant tea in Darjeeling and Ceylon. Assam is now one of the largest tea growing regions on earth, and its tea is the base of most breakfast blends.
